Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. Furthermore, we introduce a new problem concerning the uniform embeddability of spaces with an angle function into Euclidean spaces and outline its potential solutions. One significant outcome of this work is the demonstration that any betweenness space that can be conformally embedded into a Euclidean space must be embeddable as a subset of that space using a restricted notion of betweenness. Our derivation relies on the establishment of several new identities connecting the angle function, the metric, and the betweenness relation, some of which may find applications in other contexts. In particular, these identities allow for the correction of errors in the proofs of key lemmas found in the literature.

In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. To optimize the magnetic field gradient at the atom detection location, we suggest directing the superconductor's testing magnet orientation perpendicular to the interferometer's plane. Although the magnetic field deeply inside the superconductor is effectively zero, the field just above its surface can reach approximately $10^{-3}$ T. This approach offers a new technique for measuring the local magnetic field expelled from the surface of a superconductor using atomic interferometry. Since the critical field of type-II superconductors is typically around $10^{-3}$ T, this method could also be employed to determine their upper critical field. Notably, this approach is viable even when the total external magnetic field is so weak that the superconductor would normally allow magnetic field lines to penetrate its bulk.

Introduction 
The ISIC challenge is a prominent competition where teams analyze skin lesion images and metadata to classify nine distinct classes. Despite the significance of this challenge, the specific methodologies employed by various teams to compete remain undocumented. To fill this gap, we outline our methodology for the ISIC 2017, 2018, and 2019 challenges, detailing steps taken to identify the actual number of classes in the data, handling the inconsistent metadata format across years, and our ensemble of CNNs used for classification. Our contributions include a comprehensive overview of our approach for the ISIC 2017/2018/2019 challenges and open-access code for participating in these challenges.
